intro: “Ritter vom Steckenpferd” (Knight of the Hobbyhorse), No. 9 of Kinderszenen, Op. 15, depicts a child galloping on a stick horse. Its C major chords fall off the beat above a steady bass.

sections.label: A · Offbeat chords in C major
sections.mNote: The right hand starts each bar with a rest.

sections.label: B · Same rhythm at fortissimo
sections.mNote: Chromatic bass notes beneath the same bounding rhythm.

cues.title: Opening rhythm and accents
cues.text: The right hand rests on the downbeat and plays a chord halfway through the beat. Its long–short–long rhythm of crotchet, quaver and crotchet sits across the three-beat bar. Accents mark the chords.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, plate 6016, p. 13: 3/4, opening quaver rests, crotchet–quaver–crotchet chords and accents. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/f/fe/IMSLP03060-Schumann-Op015Brt6016.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Second strain
cues.text: The second part keeps the rhythm of the first unchanged. Chromatic notes enter the chords and bass, and the music later reaches fortissimo. Both halves have repeat signs.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, p. 13: two repeated strains; chromatic writing in the second, followed by fortissimo.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Letter to Raimund Härtel, 1838
cues.text: On 6 July 1838 Schumann wrote to his publisher Raimund Härtel asking for news of Kinderszenen. “They will grow too old with time,” he wrote. “Please — do not forget them; I long to see them.”
cues.evidence: Schumann to Raimund Härtel, 6 July 1838, quoted in Thomas Synofzik, 175 Jahre Kinderszenen (2013), item 6. Translation from the German. https://www.schumann-zwickau.de/media/archiv-sonderausstellungen/2013_175_Jahre_Kinderszenen.pdf

transitions.title: First strain to second strain
transitions.from: A · Offbeat chords in C major
transitions.how: The first strain closes in C major. The second keeps the right hand’s quaver rest and offbeat chords, and the left hand moves into chromatic notes. Its longer bass notes continue underneath the offbeat attacks. Later the C major chords return marked fortissimo.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, p. 13, the join between the two repeated strains and the later fortissimo return.

composer.epithet: Composer and music critic, a bookseller’s son, whose piano music depicts lovers, masks and arguments.
facts: Friedrich Wieck, piano; Heinrich Dorn, composition
Co-founded the Neue Zeitschrift für Musik in 1834; edited it until 1844
Married Clara Wieck in 1840; eight children, seven surviving infancy
composer.background:
Robert Schumann grew up among books in Zwickau. His father August sold and published them, and encouraged his son’s music; Robert read Jean Paul’s novels while learning the piano. The novels contain twins, disguises, and conversations that wander from their subject and return to it unexpectedly. In Papillons, his early set of piano dances, Schumann took up the masked ball at the end of Jean Paul’s Flegeljahre.

He went to Leipzig to study law in 1828 and moved to Heidelberg the following year. In the end he persuaded his mother to let him pursue music. Friedrich Wieck undertook to train him as a pianist. Wieck’s young daughter Clara was already performing in public; Robert was the older pupil and had more ground to make up. By 1832 paralysis in his right hand had ended his hopes of becoming a virtuoso. He studied composition with Heinrich Dorn and turned to composing and writing.
